title: Domestic breeds arise mainly by man's accumulation of successive variations

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Domestic breeds arise mainly by man's accumulation of successive variations

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Domestic breeds were not produced suddenly in their present useful form; their key cause is man's accumulative selection, nature supplying successive variations and man adding them up in directions useful to him.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The key is man’s power of accumulative selection: nature gives successive variations; man adds them up in certain directions useful to him.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter I, “Variation under Domestication”; section “Principle of Selection anciently followed, its Effects”. Scope: domesticated animals and cultivated plants

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch01-11: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.62

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Genomic time series and breeding records test several emblematic breeds, but historical coverage is uneven. The broad claim that this was the key cause across domestic forms is only partially resolvable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For breeds with archived genomes and histories, test for sequential allele-frequency shifts and polygenic selection in directions matching documented human preferences, versus sudden-origin or neutral models. Repeated cumulative directional change supports accumulative selection.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Historical breeding records are incomplete.

Selection, drift and introgression can generate overlapping signatures.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public genomes and a Mendelian catalogue can show, for major domestic species, whether breed differences look accumulated or single-step. That is a proxy for the historical mechanism, and it covers a minority of domesticated animals and plants. Mixed architectures mean the result can reject a purely sudden origin more readily than it can crown accumulative selection as the key cause.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Classify breed-defining differences by genetic architecture and by the time series of allele frequencies from ancient to modern animals: many successive small shifts versus a single large-effect origin. A predominance of multi-locus, temporally accumulated change aligned with breeding goals would support accumulative selection; a predominance of one-step sports that already match the finished breed would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Archaeological morphology cannot show that a breeder, rather than natural selection or drift, accumulated the changes.

Ancient DNA time series exist for a few species and preserve only part of the phenotype.

Both large-effect mutations and polygenic selection are real, so 'the key cause' is a balance, not a yes-or-no.
